rules.coverage_note: before_action :authenticate_user!, only: [:edit] -- the macro is the call's name and what it runs is its first argument, so the filter states which callback it names instead of only where it was written.

which method a before_action / rescue_from / helper_method actually runs: the symbol argument stripped of its leading colon is the declared method name, which is the only spelling that meets the declaration side. A macro whose argument names no method in the file does not bind here, and rails.controller.filter still states the filter.
create_table :orders, add_index :orders, :name -- the operation is the call's name and what it operates on is its first argument.

which table a migration touches: every table-shaped schema macro takes the table as its first argument, so all the migrations that create, alter or index `orders` reach one DatabaseTable. Guarded on the symbol spelling because that is the one that carries a bare name; enable_extension / disable_extension are excluded because their first argument is an extension, not a table.

belongs_to :author, has_many :comments -- the association's own name is now stated. The class it points at is not: Rails derives it by singularizing and camelizing, and the overlay has no string operation.
validates :title, scope :published, enum :status -- which attribute or scope the macro is about, not only that a macro is there.

the routing DSL entries that name something -- resources :posts, namespace :admin, mount Sidekiq::Web. `member`, `collection` and `shallow` were dropped from the list: they take a block and no argument, so they produce no call.arguments fact at all and named nothing even before.

get "/users/:id", to: "users#show" -- the HTTP method is the call's own name and the URL is its first argument, so a route is keyed by what it serves. The normalized form makes get "photos/index" and get "/photos/index" one identity, and :id, {id} and [id] agree. The symbol spelling (get :preview inside a member block) is excluded because it names an action, not a URL.
root to: "home#index" states GET / and nothing else; the method and the URL are what the macro means rather than what it spells, which is the one piece of framework knowledge this rule adds.

The block form -- `before_save do … end`, `default_scope { … }`, `resources :posts do … end`. A Ruby call needs no parentheses, so there is no argument list to read; the macro is still stated, and its argument-bearing spelling is the rule this one is named after.

`get :preview` inside a `member do … end` or `collection { … }` block. The argument is a symbol naming an action on the enclosing resource, not a URL, so the route is stated where it is written and by which verb and action; its path is the resource's and is not derivable here.

gaps: a route's handler is not stated: Rails writes it as the keyword argument to: "users#show", and omega-ruby publishes an argument only as the whole written text, so there is no key/value view of a pair argument and no string operation in the overlay to split users#show into a controller and an action
an association's target class is not stated: has_many :comments names the association, and Rails derives Comment by singularizing and camelizing it, which the overlay cannot do

the legacy get "photos/:id" => "photos#show" spelling is one association argument, so its first-argument text carries the handler as well as the URL and its Route identity is that whole text; the to: spelling and the bare-path spelling are exact
a symbol argument keeps its leading colon, because unquote strips string delimiters only, so an attribute naming an association, a table or a validated field reads :author rather than author

every Rails class is one entity under rails:class:{path}:{name}; its Rails layer is stated by a declares edge from a RailsLayer, because a canonical key holds exactly one entity kind and the first rule by id wins
Ruby visibility (private/protected) is a call, not a declaration attribute, so a controller's private helpers cannot be told apart from its actions
runtime Rails metaprogramming, dynamically loaded engines and ActiveSupport callback ordering are runtime semantics
